listening.title: Enrolling in an Evening Cooking Class
listening.context: مكالمة تسجيل في كورس طبخ مسائي. اكتب بيانات التسجيل في النموذج.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Good afternoon, Greenfield Adult Learning Centre, Karen speaking.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Hello. I'd like to enrol on one of your evening cooking classes, please. I saw a leaflet about them in the library.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Certainly. Thank you for calling. Did you find out about us from the library, then?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: My neighbour mentioned the centre too, but it was the leaflet that made me ring.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: We have two courses this term, Italian Basics and Quick Family Meals. Which one are you interested in?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Italian Basics sounds good. Is it on Tuesday evenings?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It was on Tuesdays last term, but this term it's on Wednesdays. It runs for eight weeks and the first class is on the 10th of October.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Wednesday is fine. And what time does it start?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Half past six until half past eight. Is it suitable for beginners? Yes, you don't need any experience, because Italian Basics is our beginners' course.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's a relief. I've only ever made toast and pasta. Where will the classes be held? In the main kitchen?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Normally yes, but the main kitchen is being repaired this term, so we're using the kitchen in the Science Block instead. It's just across the car park.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Okay, the Science Block. Is there parking nearby? I usually come straight from work by car.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, there's a free car park behind the building, and it's rarely full in the evenings, so you shouldn't have any trouble finding a space.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's good to know. And how much does the course cost?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The fee is £96, which includes all the ingredients.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Oh, I thought the leaflet said £86.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That was last year's price. It's £96 this term, I'm afraid, but you can pay in two instalments if you like.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's still reasonable. Let me book now.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Lovely. I'll just open the booking form on my screen. There are still a few places left, but the class is quite popular, so I'd advise booking now. Can I take your surname, please?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: It's Pemberton.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Could you spell that for me?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Of course. That's P-E-M-B-E-R-T-O-N.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Thank you, Mr Pemberton. And a contact number?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: It's 0 7 7 0 0, 9 0 0, 5 4 1. Oh, sorry, the last three digits are 5 1 4. I always mix them up.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: So that's 0 7 7 0 0, 9 0 0, 5 1 4. Is that a mobile?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes, it is.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: And your address, so that we can post the course booklet?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: It's 27 Willow Lane, in Fairfield.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Thank you. The booklet has a map of the site and a list of the dishes you'll cook. Now, one more thing. Do you have any food allergies we should know about, as you'll be handling ingredients?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes, I can't eat nuts, I'm afraid. Everything else is fine.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: I'll put that on your form so the tutor knows. Please also bring an apron and a container to take your dishes home.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Will do. Thanks very much for your help, Karen.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: You're welcome, Mr Pemberton. We look forward to seeing you on the 10th. Goodbye.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Goodbye.

listening.title: Tour of Rosewood Community Garden
listening.context: جولة إرشادية في حديقة مجتمعية. اسمع الشرح وجاوب، وبعدين حدد الأماكن على الخريطة.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Rosewood Community Garden. My name's Fiona, and I'll be showing you round for the next half hour before you decide whether you'd like to join us as a volunteer.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Let me start with a little history. The garden opened in 2009 on land that used to be a car park. People often assume the council set it up, but in fact it was started by a group of residents who wanted somewhere for local children to learn where food comes from, and it has always been run by volunteers.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: We're open from nine until five every day except Monday. The sign on the gate says we close at six in summer, but that changed this year because of the cost of lighting, so it's five all year round.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Volunteers don't have to commit to a particular day. Most people come for a couple of hours when they can, although we do ask all new volunteers to attend one short training session on a Saturday morning.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Now, if you look at the plan in front of you, we're standing at the main gate at the bottom. The gravel path goes straight ahead to the lawn at the far end.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: On your left, just inside the gate, is the tool shed. Please don't go in without a volunteer, because it's where we keep the sharp tools. Next to it is the herb garden. It used to be on the other side of the path, but we moved it last year to get more sun, and it's now the second place on the left.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Past the herb garden, in the far left-hand corner, you'll see the pond. It was dug by the children, and it's home to frogs and several kinds of dragonfly.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Now, on the right-hand side, the first building you come to is the café. It's run by a local charity, and everything is made with vegetables from the garden. Further along is the glass building, which is the greenhouse, where we grow tomatoes and chillies.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: In the far right-hand corner, opposite the pond, is the children's play area, with a sandpit and a small climbing frame.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: At the end of the path is the picnic lawn, which is a lovely place to sit on a sunny day. And finally, if you walk past the lawn and through the small wooden gate, you'll find the beehives. Please keep to the path there, and don't worry, the bees are very gentle.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Before we start walking, a quick word about what you can take home. Volunteers can take as many herbs as they like, and they also receive a free bag of vegetables every month. Visitors can buy honey and jam at the café, and plants from the greenhouse at weekends. Eggs used to be available as well, but the hens were moved to a farm last winter.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Finally, the garden is hoping to raise money for a new roof for the tool shed, as the old one leaks in heavy rain. We've collected about two thirds of the amount we need, so any donations at the end of the tour would be very welcome.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right, if everyone's ready, let's head down the path, and I'll show you the herb garden first.

listening.title: Project Meeting about Public Libraries
listening.context: نقاش بين طالبين ومشرفهم عن مشروع بحثي. ركّز مين بيقول إيه.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: Come in, both of you. So, how's the project on public libraries going?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Quite well, Dr Hughes. We've used five main sources, but some of them have been more useful than others.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes. The library's own website was the first one we tried. It has a lot of statistics about visitors, but most of the figures stop in 2016, so we can't really use them for a current picture.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: That's a pity. What about the census data?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: It shows how the population around each library has changed, which is exactly what we need. The problem is that the tables were quite difficult to understand at first, but Maya worked out how to read them.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: And the newspaper archive was interesting, but you need a subscription, which is fifteen pounds a month, so we only paid for one week.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: Fair enough. And your own questionnaire?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: We only got thirty replies, and they were all from students on our course, so I don't think it tells us much about the wider public.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: Well, you can say that in your limitations section. What about the librarian you interviewed?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That was the best source by far. She gave us figures we couldn't find anywhere else, and she explained why one branch had lost visitors.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: Which was?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: In that town the library cut its opening hours from sixty to thirty-five hours a week, and the number of visitors fell by almost a third. It wasn't the new bus route, which is what we first thought.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: Good. That's a clear finding. Now, let's talk about the report itself. How do you plan to begin?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: I thought we could start with a personal story about how I learned to read in the library as a child.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: It's a nice idea, but a personal story is better for a talk than for a written report. I'd suggest opening with a surprising fact instead, such as the number of people who still use libraries every year. It makes the reader want to continue.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That makes sense. And how should we present the results? Maya wanted a poster.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Actually, I've changed my mind. A slideshow will let us include graphs, and the graphs will show the changes over time much more clearly.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: I agree, a slideshow is the better choice.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: My main worry is the deadline. The report is due on the 18th of November, and we still haven't finished the analysis. I'm not sure we'll be ready.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: You have three weeks, which is enough if you divide the work sensibly. Don't be tempted to add extra sources now.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Should we include the full questionnaire in the report?

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: Put it in an appendix at the end. The examiner will want to see it, but it would interrupt the flow of your argument if it were in the main text. Come and see me again next Thursday and bring a draft of the results section.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: We will. Thank you, Dr Hughes.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Thanks very much.

listening.title: Lecture: Green Roofs in Cities
listening.context: محاضرة جامعية عن الأسطح الخضراء في المدن. كمّل الملاحظات وجاوب.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Good morning. Today I'd like to talk about green roofs, which are roofs covered with plants growing in a thin layer of soil. The idea isn't new. Turf roofs were common on farm buildings in Scandinavia for centuries, but the modern version was developed in Germany in the 1960s, and it has since spread across the world.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Let me begin with the benefits. The first is temperature. In summer, a green roof can lower the temperature inside a building by up to five degrees, because the plants and soil block the heat that a dark roof would absorb. That means less air conditioning, and lower electricity bills.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The second benefit concerns rain. A green roof acts like a sponge. It can absorb up to seventy per cent of the rain that falls on it, which reduces the amount of water rushing into the drains during a storm. In cities that suffer from flooding, this is extremely valuable.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Which plants are best? Most designers choose a low-growing plant called sedum. It stores water in its leaves, survives long dry periods and needs very little soil, so the roof doesn't have to be especially strong. People often worry that green roofs are too heavy, but modern systems weigh no more than a layer of gravel, so weight is rarely the problem.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: So why doesn't every building have one? The main reason is cost. A green roof is more expensive to install than an ordinary roof, and one of the most important parts is a special membrane that stops roots from damaging the building. If it is fitted badly, leaks can be very difficult to repair, so it has to be done by specialists.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: There is also the question of maintenance. Although a green roof doesn't need watering, it does need weeding twice a year, to stop larger plants, such as young trees, taking over. In a block of flats, the residents usually pay for this through their service charge.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: On the other hand, there are financial incentives. Some city councils offer owners a tax reduction if they install a green roof, because the whole neighbourhood benefits from the cooler air and the lower risk of floods.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Now, what about the future? Some people are excited about growing vegetables on roofs, and there are certainly successful examples. Others focus on saving energy. But personally, I believe the greatest long-term benefit will be cleaner air. Plants trap dust and absorb pollution, and as more cities introduce limits on traffic, green roofs could make a real difference to the health of people who live in crowded areas.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: To summarise, then, green roofs keep buildings cooler, protect cities from floods, and help wildlife, although they cost more at the start. For next week, I'd like you to read the two articles on the course website, and think about whether a green roof would be suitable for our own faculty building.

**Pinewood Lake Campsite: Visitor Information**

**Arrival and departure**

Reception is open from 8.00 am to 8.00 pm every day between April and October. Guests may arrive after 2.00 pm and must leave by 11.00 am on the day of departure. Anyone arriving after 8.00 pm should telephone the duty manager in advance so that a gate code can be arranged.

**Pitches and prices**

A standard tent pitch costs £18 per night, and a pitch with an electric hook-up costs £24. Children under five stay free of charge. A discount of 10% is given to anyone who books for seven nights or more. Caravans and motorhomes are welcome but must be booked at least two weeks ahead, because only six pitches are large enough.

**Facilities**

The shower block is located behind the shop and is cleaned three times a day. Hot showers are included in the price, but a token for the laundry machines costs £1. The shop sells basic groceries, firewood and gas bottles, and it closes at 6.00 pm. The lake is open for swimming from June to September; there is no lifeguard, so parents must supervise their children at all times.

**Rules**

Campfires are not permitted anywhere on the site, but portable gas barbecues may be used on the grass area beside the lake. Dogs are welcome if kept on a lead, though they are not allowed in the shop. Quiet hours begin at 10.30 pm, and music must be turned off by then. Visitors who break these rules may be asked to leave.

Six weekly sessions for people who have been supervisors for less than a year. Each participant is matched with an experienced mentor from another department. The course ends with a short presentation to the management team about a real workplace project.

reading.title: The Return of the Local Market
reading.text:
**A**

In many towns, the weekly market was once the heart of community life. Farmers brought vegetables, eggs and cheese to the central square, and families met there to exchange news as much as to shop. By the 1980s, however, supermarkets with car parks, low prices and long opening hours had drawn customers away, and many markets shrank to a handful of stalls or closed altogether. In some towns the square was turned into a car park, and a generation of young people grew up without ever seeing a fish stall or a cheese counter. For a time, it seemed that the market had become a thing of the past.

**B**

In recent years, the tide has turned. Across Europe and North America, new markets open every year, and old ones that had been written off are crowded again on Saturday mornings. Surveys suggest that the main reason is not price. Shoppers say they value freshness, the chance to talk to the person who grew the food, and a sense of knowing where it came from. A market in the north of England, for example, reports that its number of weekly visitors has doubled in ten years, even though a basket of shopping there often costs a little more than the same goods at the nearest supermarket. Organisers also point to the atmosphere, with musicians, bakers calling out to passers-by, and children running between the stalls.

**C**

Traders have noticed a change in the kind of customer who visits. Whereas older shoppers once came mainly to save money, many of today's buyers are young professionals who are willing to pay more for something special. One cheese seller, who started with a single table in 2012, now employs six people. 'People want a story with their food,' she says. 'They like to hear how the cows are looked after.' Another trader, who sells vegetables grown on a small farm outside the city, says that half of her customers now ask which field their potatoes came from, something that would have seemed strange to her parents. Many young buyers also arrive with their own cloth bags, because they dislike plastic packaging.

**D**

Not everybody is convinced that the revival is as healthy as it looks. Some so-called farmers' markets are supplied by wholesalers rather than farms, and a stall labelled 'local' may have travelled hundreds of kilometres to reach the square. It is hard to avoid the conclusion that some stallholders are taking advantage of shoppers' trust. Several city councils have responded by sending inspectors to check where the produce really comes from. Stallholders who pass the checks receive a certificate to display, which they say has been good for business, although the cost of inspections is paid from public money.

**E**

Markets also bring benefits beyond food. Research at an Australian university found that people who shop at a market have on average several times more conversations during a visit than those who shop at a supermarket. For older residents who live alone, the weekly trip can be a main source of social contact. Some markets now offer a free coffee morning for retired visitors, which has proved popular. Doctors in one region have even begun to suggest a regular market visit to patients who feel lonely, arguing that a short walk, some fresh air and a friendly conversation can improve a person's mood in a way that medicine cannot.

**F**

The economics, though, are fragile. Stallholders must get up before dawn, pay rent to the market operator and depend on the weather, since a wet Saturday can halve a day's takings. In response, a number of markets have moved into covered halls, which is a sensible step, and some have added evening events with street food and music. These attract crowds all year round and allow traders to earn more. Others have formed co-operatives so that members can share the cost of transport and storage, which is especially useful for small producers who would otherwise find it impossible to sell outside their own village.

**G**

Looking ahead, many planners believe that markets will have a place in the future of towns, not as a nostalgic exhibit but as practical meeting spaces. A growing number of new housing developments now reserve land for a market square, and online ordering for collection at the stall is proving popular. Whether markets can keep their special character as they grow is the question that traders worry about most. If rents rise too far, small producers may be pushed out, and the market could end up resembling the shopping centres it was meant to replace.

task2.prompt:
Write about the following topic:
Some people think that all children should learn how to cook at school. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
Write at least 250 words.
task2.modelAnswer:
In many countries, young people leave school without knowing how to prepare a simple meal. I strongly agree that cooking should be a compulsory part of the school curriculum, because it teaches practical skills, encourages healthier eating habits and prepares children for independent life.

Firstly, cooking is one of the most useful skills a person can have, yet it is rarely taught at home when parents are busy. A teenager who has learned how to follow a recipe, measure ingredients and use a kitchen safely will feel far more confident when he or she moves out to study or work. In addition, cooking involves reading, maths and teamwork, so lessons can support what pupils learn in other subjects.

Secondly, children who cook for themselves tend to understand food better. If they know how much sugar and salt goes into a ready meal, they are more likely to choose fresh ingredients later in life. This matters because poor diets are a growing cause of health problems around the world, and schools are one of the few places where all children can be reached. For example, a school in my own city introduced a weekly cooking class, and teachers reported that pupils began to bring fruit rather than sweets for their lunch.

Admittedly, there are some arguments against the idea. Cooking lessons need equipment and space, which some schools cannot afford, and the timetable is already crowded. However, these problems can be solved with simple recipes that need little equipment, and by giving cooking the same importance as other practical subjects such as art or sport.

In conclusion, learning to cook gives children skills for life and helps them to make better decisions about what they eat. For these reasons, I believe schools should teach it to every child, and governments should give them the support they need to do so.

listening.title: Lecture: Coral Reefs under Pressure
listening.context: محاضرة عن الشعاب المرجانية. كمّل الملاحظات.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Today's lecture is about coral reefs, which are often described as the rainforests of the sea. Reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they provide a home for about a quarter of all marine species, which makes them extraordinarily important.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: First, what exactly is a coral? Each coral is a tiny animal called a polyp. Polyps build a hard skeleton of limestone around themselves, and over thousands of years these skeletons form the reef. Inside the tissue of each polyp live microscopic algae, and the relationship works in both directions. The algae use sunlight to produce food for the coral, and in return the coral provides protection.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: This is why most reefs are found in shallow water, usually no deeper than about thirty metres. Below that, there isn't enough light for the algae. Reefs also need warm water, between twenty-three and twenty-nine degrees, and when the temperature rises just a little above the usual level, the coral becomes stressed and expels the algae. The result is called bleaching, because the coral loses its colour and turns white.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Bleaching doesn't always kill the coral. If the water cools within a few weeks, the algae can return. But repeated bleaching events leave little time for recovery, and some reefs have lost more than half their coral in a single decade.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Temperature is not the only threat. Run-off from farmland carries fertiliser into coastal water, which feeds seaweed that grows over the coral and blocks the light. Fishing with explosives, which is still practised in some regions, destroys the structure of the reef completely, and it can take decades to recover.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: So what is being done? One approach is to protect the best reefs by creating marine parks, where fishing is limited. A second approach is restoration. Scientists collect fragments of healthy coral, grow them in nurseries for about a year, and then attach them to damaged reefs. It's slow work, and it cannot replace a reef that has been lost, but it gives some areas a second chance.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The third approach is the most interesting. Researchers are testing corals that are more tolerant of heat, and some teams are trying to breed them. The aim isn't to create a perfect super coral, but to give reefs a better chance as the oceans warm.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: There's also a role for tourism. Divers who pay to visit a reef have a financial interest in keeping it healthy, and in some countries the fees they pay are used to employ local people as rangers. The biggest danger here is crowding. Too many visitors touching the coral or kicking up sand can cause damage, so many operators now limit the number of divers per day.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: To sum up, reefs are fragile but not helpless. Your reading for next time is the case study on the island marine park, and please bring any questions about how restoration projects are funded.

reading.text:
**Maplewood Public Library: Services and Rules**

**Joining**

Membership is free for everyone who lives, works or studies in the Maplewood area. To join, bring a photo identity card and one document showing your home address, such as a recent bill. Children under twelve must be accompanied by an adult when they register. Your library card will be issued on the same day.

**Borrowing**

Members may borrow up to twelve books at a time for three weeks. DVDs and music CDs may be borrowed for one week only, with a limit of three items per person. Items can be renewed twice, either online or at the desk, unless another member has reserved them. A charge of 20p per day is made for each overdue book, but there is no charge for children's books.

**Computers and study space**

Free internet access is available on the first floor, and sessions last a maximum of one hour. Printing costs 10p per page for black and white and 40p for colour. The quiet study room on the second floor can be reserved in advance by phone for up to three hours. Eating is not allowed anywhere in the library, though drinks in sealed bottles may be brought into the café area.

**Special events**

A reading group for adults meets on the last Thursday of every month at 6.30 pm. On Saturday mornings, volunteers read stories to children aged three to six in the children's section. No booking is necessary for either event, although the reading group has a limit of fifteen members.

reading.title: How We Find Our Way
reading.text:
**A**

Every day, millions of people walk or drive through places they know well without giving a thought to the route. Only when something goes wrong, such as a closed road or a missing sign, do we realise how much mental work is involved. Navigation seems simple, yet it is one of the most complex tasks the human brain performs, and scientists have spent decades trying to understand how it works.

**B**

Long before maps existed, travellers found their way by reading the natural world. Polynesian sailors crossed thousands of kilometres of open ocean by observing the position of the stars, the direction of swells and the flight paths of birds. Desert nomads recognised the shape of dunes and the direction of the prevailing wind. These skills were passed from one generation to the next, and they allowed people to travel with remarkable accuracy without any instruments. A navigator on a traditional canoe might sit for days with little sleep, keeping an exact mental record of every change in wind and current, and so knowing the position of the boat at all times without writing a single note.

**C**

In the 1970s, researchers working in London discovered cells in a part of the brain called the hippocampus that become active when an animal is in a particular place. Different cells respond to different locations, so that together they build a kind of internal map. Later work found other cells that act like a grid, helping to measure distance. The discoveries were considered so important that they were later recognised with a major scientific prize.

**D**

The most famous study of navigation in humans involved London taxi drivers, who must memorise around twenty-five thousand streets to obtain their licence. Brain scans showed that the part of the hippocampus used for spatial memory was larger in the drivers than in the average person, and that it grew in size as they gained experience. Interestingly, it was smaller in retired drivers, suggesting that the brain adapts to what we regularly use.

**E**

The design of a city also affects how easily we find our way. In places where streets are laid out in a regular grid, as in many North American cities, people usually form a clear mental picture and can estimate directions with ease. In older European towns, where lanes curve and meet at odd angles, visitors are more likely to become disoriented. Distinctive landmarks, such as a tall church tower, help enormously, because they give the mind a fixed point of reference. A study in one European city found that visitors who were shown a photograph of a landmark before setting out reached their destination faster than those who were given only a street name. Modern buildings of glass and steel, which look almost identical, can be far more confusing than an old house with a red door.

**F**

Many people now rely on satellite navigation, and this raises an important question. Researchers who tested drivers found that those who followed spoken instructions remembered less about the route afterwards than those who used a paper map. It would be an exaggeration to claim that technology makes us worse at navigating, but it seems clear that we pay less attention to our surroundings when a device gives us the answers. Some drivers admit that after using satellite navigation for years, they can no longer find their way to a friend's house without it, even though they have visited it many times. Others say that the device has given them the confidence to travel to unfamiliar places that they would previously have avoided, which is a clear advantage.

**G**

The good news is that spatial skills can be improved. People who deliberately explore new neighbourhoods without a phone, or who practise drawing a map from memory, tend to develop a stronger sense of direction. Some experts recommend turning off the navigation app on familiar journeys. They argue that, just as muscles weaken when they are not used, the brain's navigation system benefits from regular exercise, and that a little effort now may protect our abilities as we age. Schools, too, are beginning to take an interest, with some teachers taking children on orienteering days in which pupils must find their way around a park using only a simple map and a compass. Early results suggest that the children enjoy the challenge and remember the layout of the area much better than expected.

task2.prompt:
Write about the following topic:
Some people believe that museums and art galleries should be free for everyone. Others think that visitors should pay an entrance fee. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
Write at least 250 words.
task2.modelAnswer:
Whether public museums should charge admission is a question that divides opinion. Some argue that culture belongs to everyone and should be free, while others believe that fees are necessary to keep these institutions running. In my view, a balanced system, in which entry to the permanent collection is free but special exhibitions are charged, offers the best solution.

Those who support free entry make a convincing argument. Museums preserve the heritage of a nation, and it seems unfair that families on low incomes should be unable to see it. When the British government abolished fees at national museums in 2001, visitor numbers rose sharply, and many of the new visitors were young people who might otherwise never have gone. Free access also allows people to make short visits, such as dropping in for an hour during lunch, without feeling that they must get their money's worth.

On the other hand, running a museum is expensive. Buildings must be heated, collections must be protected, and staff must be paid. If governments reduce funding, as they often do during economic difficulties, the museum may have to cut opening hours or even sell items. Charging a modest fee ensures a steady income and allows the museum to improve its facilities. Moreover, people who pay often value the experience more, and may treat the displays with greater respect.

Personally, I believe the best approach combines the two ideas. A free permanent collection guarantees that nobody is excluded, while paid temporary exhibitions, which are costly to organise, can bring in the money needed. Donation boxes and members' schemes can add further support.

In conclusion, although both sides have valid points, I think that access to cultural heritage should not depend on a person's income. A mixed system protects this principle without placing too heavy a burden on the museum's budget.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Some of you may remember that the hall was built in 1927 as a covered fish market. When it closed in the nineties, there was a proposal to turn it into a car park, but local campaigners fought the plan, and in the end, the council agreed to restore the building, with the help of a lottery grant.

lines.text: The work has taken fourteen months, which is four months longer than we promised, mainly because the roof needed more repairs than the surveyors expected. The hall will open to the public on the first Saturday in October. The ceremony was going to be at ten, but the mayor can't attend then, so it will start at noon instead.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Now let me guide you through the layout on your plan. As you come in through the main entrance, you'll see the central aisle running straight ahead to the open area at the end.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: On your left, immediately inside the entrance, is the information desk, where visitors can pick up a map. The next unit along on the left is the bakery. We originally planned to put the flower stall there, but the bakers wanted to be near the entrance, so the flowers have moved further up. At the far end of the left side, in the corner, you'll find the fishmonger, which seems fitting, given the history of the hall.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Opposite the information desk, on the right, will be the fruit and vegetable stall. Beside it, in the middle on the right, is the café, which has big windows facing the river. The corner unit at the far end on the right is the flower stall.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: At the end of the aisle is the open area, which will be used for demonstrations and music. The toilets are just beyond the open area, accessible from the side door.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: There's one more facility I'd like to mention: the repair kiosk. This is a new idea. Volunteers will mend small items, such as broken toasters and torn clothes, free of charge. It's in the loading yard behind the hall, in a converted shipping container, which is reached through the door at the back of the open area.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Parking is limited, so we're encouraging people to arrive by bus or by bike. There will be space for two hundred bicycles and a cycle repair stand, and the number fourteen bus will stop outside the door every ten minutes. For those who must drive, there's a car park a five-minute walk away, which costs two pounds for the whole day.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Finally, if you'd like to support the hall, there are three ways. You can volunteer at the repair kiosk, you can become a Friend of the Market and receive a discount card, or you can sponsor one of the stalls for a small trader. Details are available at the information desk, and I'll be happy to answer any questions now.

listening.title: Discussing a Study of Language-Learning Apps
listening.context: نقاش مع المشرف حول بحث عن تطبيقات تعلم اللغات.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: Come in, Chloe, Dev. I've read your proposal on language-learning apps. Before we talk about methods, I'd like to hear about your own experience, Chloe, since you've used several.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, I have, Dr Okafor. The streak counter was great for the first month, because I hated breaking a chain, but then it started to feel like pressure rather than motivation, and I found it quite annoying.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I felt the same about the leaderboards. They're meant to be competitive, but half the people on mine were obviously just trying to gain points quickly without actually learning anything.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: Interesting. Chloe, did the voice recognition feature help?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It surprised me, actually. I thought it would be useless, but when it marked a word as wrong, I repeated it until it was right, and my pronunciation improved a lot, which I never expected from a free app.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: And the reminders?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Honestly, I turned those off after a week. I'd rather decide when to study. The offline mode I barely touched, because I always had internet on the train.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: For me, the best results came from using the app alongside weekly lessons with a tutor. The app handled vocabulary, and the tutor corrected my mistakes, which the app can't do properly. I think that combination is the most effective approach.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: That's a hypothesis you could test. Now, what about the premium version? Did either of you pay for it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: I did, for six months, at nine pounds a month. It removed adverts and unlocked extra lessons, but I'm not sure it was worth it.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: Right. Let's turn to your method. You're proposing to compare two groups of learners over eight weeks. What's your main concern, Dev?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That people will drop out. In most studies of apps, over half the participants stop using them after a few weeks, and that would leave us with a very small sample.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: It's a real problem. One solution is to offer a small reward, such as a gift voucher, to everyone who completes the study.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That might bias the results, though, if they're only doing it for the voucher. I'm more concerned that we have no way of checking how much the participants actually study. We rely on their own reports.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: You could use the data the app records itself. Most apps allow users to download their activity history. It would be more objective than a questionnaire.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's a good idea. We hadn't thought of that.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: Finally, think about how you'll measure progress. A vocabulary test is easy to administer, but it only captures one part of language ability. I'd recommend adding a short speaking task, even though it will take longer to mark.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: We could record each participant for two minutes and ask a second marker to score it.

lines.speaker: C
lines.text: Good. Send me a revised plan by the end of next week, and we'll look at the ethics form together.

listening.title: Lecture: Microplastics in Freshwater
listening.context: محاضرة عن الجزيئات البلاستيكية الدقيقة في المياه العذبة.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Public attention has focused on plastic in the oceans, but in the last decade researchers have turned their attention to rivers and lakes, which are where most of the plastic enters the sea. Today I'll look at what we know about microplastics in freshwater, which are fragments less than five millimetres long.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: There are two main types. Primary microplastics are made small on purpose, for example the tiny beads once used in face washes, which are now banned in many countries. Secondary microplastics come from larger objects, such as bottles and bags, which break down gradually under sunlight and wave action. Secondary fragments are far more common.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A surprising source is clothing. When synthetic fabrics such as polyester are washed, they release thousands of tiny fibres. A single load of laundry can release up to seven hundred thousand fibres, and most wastewater plants cannot filter them all, so they pass into rivers.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Tyres are another major source. As a car travels, its tyres wear down, and the dust is washed from the road into drains during rain. In some studies, tyre particles were found to make up more than half of the microplastics in urban streams.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Now, what is the impact on living things? Fish and insect larvae mistake the particles for food. In laboratory experiments, small fish that ate plastic grew more slowly, but one important point is that these experiments often use concentrations much higher than those found in nature, so we should be careful when interpreting the results.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A related concern is that plastic can carry chemicals. Particles can absorb pollutants from the water, and they might release them inside an animal's body. The evidence for this is still limited, and some researchers think that food and water contain larger amounts of these chemicals than the plastic itself does.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: What about human health? Microplastics have been found in drinking water and in bottled water. At present, there's no clear evidence that the amounts we consume are harmful, but scientists emphasise that long-term studies are lacking. Therefore the prudent approach is to reduce exposure while research continues.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: There are practical steps. Washing machine filters, which cost around thirty pounds, can capture up to ninety per cent of fibres, and some countries are considering making them compulsory in new machines. Wastewater plants are also being upgraded with finer filters, although it's an expensive process which will take many years.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Some governments have also introduced regulations, requiring manufacturers to label clothing that sheds large quantities of fibres. That information helps consumers to make informed choices at the point of sale.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: On an individual level, you can wash clothes less often, at lower temperatures, and choose natural fabrics such as cotton or wool. For next week, please read the paper on river sampling methods, and think about how you would design a survey of a lake near your own home.

reading.title: Harwood Self-Storage: Customer Information
reading.text:
**Harwood Self-Storage: Customer Information**

**Renting a unit**

Units are available in four sizes, from a small locker of one square metre to a large room of fifteen square metres. Rental is monthly, and the first four weeks are half price for new customers. A refundable deposit equal to one month's rent is required when you sign the agreement, and it will be returned within ten days of your moving out, provided the unit is left clean and undamaged.

**Access**

The site is open for access between 7.00 am and 9.00 pm, seven days a week, including public holidays. Customers have their own door code, which must not be shared with anybody else. Vehicles may be driven up to the doors of ground-floor units, but upper-floor customers should use the trolleys provided at the entrance.

**Insurance**

Your belongings are not automatically insured by Harwood. You can either arrange cover through your own household policy or buy our own insurance, which costs £3 a month for each £1,000 of goods stored. Customers who choose our policy must list the main items in the storage inventory form.

**What you may not store**

For safety reasons, storing fuel, gas bottles, fireworks or any other hazardous materials is strictly forbidden. Food and live animals may not be stored. Customers who break these rules will be asked to remove their belongings within 48 hours. We also do not allow customers to live or sleep in their units.

reading.text:
**Employee Benefits at Orchard & Lane**

All staff may choose from the following options. Benefits can be changed once a year, in January.

**A. Cycle-to-Work Scheme**

Employees can obtain a bicycle and safety equipment worth up to £1,200 through the company, repaying the cost out of their monthly salary before tax. Bicycles must be bought from approved suppliers only. The scheme is open to everyone who has completed their probationary period.

**B. Private Health Cover**

The company pays for basic cover for the employee. Members of the employee's family can be added if the employee pays an additional monthly premium. Cover begins after three months of employment, and applies only to staff on permanent contracts.

**C. Study Support Fund**

Employees may claim up to £1,500 a year towards the cost of a recognised course related to their role. Claims must be supported by proof of enrolment, and employees who leave within twelve months of completing a course must repay half of the fee.

**D. Extra Holiday Purchase**

Staff can buy up to five additional days of annual leave, with the cost deducted from their salary in twelve equal instalments. Requests must be made before the start of the tax year, and unused days cannot be carried over.

**E. Childcare Vouchers**

Parents of children under eleven can receive vouchers worth up to £250 a month, which can be exchanged for nursery or after-school club fees at registered providers. The company covers the full amount, but employees must renew their application every six months.

reading.title: Hybrid Working Policy: Office Zones
reading.text:
**Hybrid Working Policy: Office Zones**

**Introduction**

From January, all teams will work a hybrid pattern, with a minimum of two days a week in the office. To make the best use of space, desks can no longer be assigned to individuals, and staff will book a place in one of four zones through the company app. Bookings can be made up to two weeks in advance and cancelled up to 8.00 am on the day.

**The four zones**

The Quiet Zone, on the third floor, is for work that demands concentration. Phone calls and conversations are not permitted, and food must not be brought in. The Collaboration Zone on the second floor has large tables and whiteboards, and it is designed for team meetings and workshops. On the first floor, the Focus Booths are individual sound-proof rooms that can be reserved for up to two hours at a time, mainly for video calls. The Social Zone on the ground floor includes the café and sofas, where staff are encouraged to eat lunch and meet colleagues from other departments.

**Lockers and equipment**

Each employee receives a locker in the basement, which should be emptied at the end of every week. Laptops and monitors are provided at every desk, but employees who need special equipment, such as an adjustable chair, should apply to the facilities team in advance.

**Etiquette**

Employees who fail to attend a booked place three times in a month will lose the right to book in advance for the following month. Staff are asked to leave desks clean and to clear all personal belongings at the end of the day.

reading.title: Rethinking the Open-Plan Office
reading.text:
**A**

When the first open-plan offices appeared in Germany in the late 1950s, they were designed to break down hierarchy. Managers and junior staff sat in a single large room, desks were arranged in flowing patterns instead of rows, and the intention was that information would pass more freely between departments. The concept soon spread to the United States and then across the world, and by the end of the century, it had become the standard layout for large companies.

**B**

It was not long before the economic advantages became obvious. A large room without walls costs far less to build, heat and reconfigure than a series of separate offices, and more employees can be fitted into the same floor area. Managers were quick to promote the open plan as a modern way of encouraging collaboration, though some critics suspected that the real motive was to save money, and that talk of teamwork was simply a convenient justification. In several large firms, the number of square metres allowed for each employee fell by a third within a decade, and the savings were often reported to shareholders as an achievement.

**C**

Yet the research that has accumulated over several decades presents a more complicated picture. In one widely cited study, a team of Harvard researchers tracked employees at two companies before and after they moved to open-plan space. Far from increasing face-to-face conversation, the change reduced it by about seventy per cent, as workers put on headphones and communicated by email instead. Having lost privacy, they appear to have created it for themselves. A second study, carried out in a Danish company, found that employees in an open space took more sick days than colleagues in smaller rooms, perhaps because illnesses spread more easily when hundreds of people share the same air and surfaces.

**D**

Interruption is a particular problem. Psychologists have found that after being distracted, a person may need more than twenty minutes to return fully to a task, and in a crowded room, distractions are almost constant. The sound of speech is especially disruptive, since the brain automatically attends to language even when we try to ignore it. Many workers say they stay late or arrive early simply to enjoy a few quiet hours, which suggests that the layout may be hurting rather than helping their output. One manager, who measured the work completed by a team before and after a move, was surprised to find that the busiest, most talkative days were often the least productive, since the staff spent so much time dealing with each other's questions.

**E**

Not all of the findings are negative, however. Some studies show that younger employees, and those whose jobs are largely social, report higher satisfaction in open spaces and enjoy the sense of belonging that comes from being surrounded by colleagues. The difficulty is that every office contains people with different personalities and tasks. A layout that suits an energetic salesperson may be a source of constant frustration for an accountant preparing a complicated tax return. Personality plays a part as well, as quieter people often find the constant presence of others tiring, whereas outgoing colleagues say they feel isolated when they are shut in a room.

**F**

Some organisations have therefore adopted what is known as activity-based working. Instead of a personal desk, employees choose a setting according to the task: a silent area for writing, a lounge for informal chats, a phone booth for calls. In theory, the model offers the best of both worlds. In practice, it has met resistance, since many staff dislike having to carry their belongings around and resent the loss of a space they could call their own. Surveys of employees in such offices show a mixed response, and few companies have reported a dramatic improvement in productivity. Some workers have reacted by arriving early to claim the best seats, which defeats the purpose of the system.

**G**

Where does this leave the open-plan office? It would be foolish to dismiss it entirely, since it plainly suits certain businesses and certain people. But the evidence suggests that managers should stop assuming that it is a universal solution. A thoughtful design would offer a variety of spaces and give workers genuine control over where they sit, and perhaps the most valuable step is simply to ask employees what they need before changing the layout, rather than after.

A friend from another country is coming to stay with you for a week next month. Write a letter to your friend. In your letter:
- say how you are looking forward to the visit
- suggest some things you could do together
- ask what he or she would like to see or do

task1.modelAnswer:
Dear Sam,

It was wonderful to hear that you are finally coming to visit me next month. I have been looking forward to it ever since you told me, and I have already cleared out the spare room so that you will be comfortable.

I have been thinking about how we could spend the week. If the weather is good, we could take a day trip to the old fort by the sea, which has beautiful views and a lovely little fish restaurant. You always liked old buildings, so I would also like to take you to the museum in the city centre. In the evenings, we could just relax at home, or go to the open-air cinema in the park, which I know you would love. If you are feeling energetic, there is a great hiking trail only an hour away.

Of course, these are only suggestions. Please let me know if there is anything in particular that you would like to see or do, and whether you have any food that you cannot eat, so that I can plan the meals.

Send me your flight details when you have them, and I will meet you at the airport. I can't wait to see you!

Best wishes,
Karim

task2.prompt:
Write about the following topic:
In many countries, an increasing number of people live alone. Why is this happening? Is it a positive or a negative development?
Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
Write at least 250 words.
task2.modelAnswer:
Across much of the world, one-person households are becoming steadily more common. This trend has several causes, and although it brings some benefits, I believe that on balance it is a negative development unless societies take steps to prevent isolation.

The rise in solo living can be explained by a combination of economic and social changes. Firstly, people are marrying later, and more marriages end in divorce, so adults spend a larger part of their lives without a partner. Secondly, rising incomes mean that many young professionals can afford their own flat, whereas in previous generations they would have shared with family or friends. Finally, people are living longer, and when a partner dies, an older person often remains in the family home alone. In Japan and Sweden, for example, around forty per cent of households now contain only one person.

There are certainly some advantages. Those who live alone enjoy independence, privacy and the freedom to organise their lives as they wish. For some, living alone is a deliberate and happy choice. In addition, the growing demand for small homes can encourage developers to build more compact and efficient housing.

However, the disadvantages are more significant. Loneliness is associated with depression, heart disease and a shorter life expectancy, and people who live alone are at greater risk of being isolated, particularly if they are elderly or have recently moved to a new city. Furthermore, one-person households use more energy and space per person than larger ones, which adds to environmental pressure.

For these reasons, I regard the trend with some concern. Nevertheless, its negative effects can be reduced if governments and communities create social opportunities, such as shared gardens, community centres and neighbourhood clubs. If these measures are in place, living alone need not mean being alone.
